Hi,
I'd like to contribute to CSLib! From what I've seen, there is no formalization of graphs or graph algorithms (beyond this PR that introduces ad-hoc definitions).
Would this be interest, and is there an ongoing effort?

The idea is to have generic, reusable definitions for graphs (directed, weighted), basic properties (shortest paths, reachability, connectivity, etc.). We could then use these definitions to prove correctness of graph algorithms.
As a byproduct of this work, we would implement and formalize of several data structures (binary heap, union find) used in these algorithms.

Also, is there currently a framework for working with time complexity in CSLib?
There’s ongoing discussion on what the lightweight framework is going to be.

Graphs are defined in mathlib and I guess we should try to use these definitions as much as possible to be more robust. The framework for time complexity is right now a point of discussion here #CSLib > Algorithm frameworks (TimeM, cslib#372, cslib#376)
The language Boole is likely to be the heavyweight implementation focussed version.
On the other hand when I worked with a graph algorithm the adjancency matrix formalization of mathlib was not the best choice
And fwiw the distributed graph algorithms community is pursuing its own formalization library outside CSLib.
Many of us are currently in a workshop in Italy revisiting our model hierarchy

Does that mean that, in the long run, algorithms should be implemented in Boole and formalized in Lean?

Gabriel Bathie said:

Shreyas Srinivas said :

The language Boole is likely to be the heavyweight implementation focussed version.

Does that mean that, in the long run, algorithms should be implemented in Boole and formalized in Lean?

Depends on what you care about. A lot of algorithms research just works at a much higher level than the RAM model by building on top of algorithms from existing literature. Our (cslib#372) model is trying to do a lightweight monadic top down formalization where we explicitly state custom models and costs upfront. And then others can independently state reductions from custom models to basic models.
Boole is (per presentations introducing CSLib in July 2025) focused on producing verified implementations from the get go.

So if you are an algorithms theorist who wants to focus on the relevant parts of theory in a STOC paper, I’d say pick our approach. If you really care about implementable algorithms for a different area of research or well… just verifying implementation of algorithms, Boole is your goal. As far as undergrad curricula typically go, implementability is not an issue. It’s when you start touching research papers that the gap between theory and implementation grows enough to accommodate an entire nearly separate area of research. A bottom up approach will take years to get to frontier papers. In fact it will not ever happen for a lot of theory models which are artefacts constructed to study specific properties of algorithms in a simplified setting. For this a top down approach is better. We just plan to work modularly through a hierarchy of models down to basic models. The papers themselves rely on the literature for the reduction to basic models.
There are other benefits to the top down approach. But I’ll save that for another chat.
